Can we trust cheap air quality sensors?

Calibration, drift, forecasting and honest uncertainty for a low-cost sensor box, using 9,357 hours of roadside measurements next to reference-grade analysers.

Data: UCI Air Quality (De Vito et al., 2008), one station in an Italian city, 2004-03-10 to 2005-04-04. Every number on this page is produced by python run_all.py.

1. The problem

Reference-grade air quality monitors are accurate, expensive and sparse. Low-cost sensor boxes are cheap enough to put on every street, which is why networks of them now feed public air quality maps. Their weakness is trust: the sensors respond to several gases at once, to temperature and to humidity, and their response changes with time.

This dataset is a year of exactly that situation. A box with five metal-oxide sensors sat beside certified analysers for CO, NOx, NO2 and benzene. That allows four practical questions to be answered with data:

  • How well can the cheap sensors be calibrated to reproduce the reference instruments?
  • How quickly does that calibration go stale, and can staleness be detected without a reference?
  • Can NO2 be forecast hours ahead well enough to beat simple rules of thumb?
  • Can the forecast say how sure it is, and raise a warning before the legal limit is exceeded?

2. What the original evaluation measured

The first version of this project reported R² of 0.99 for tree models predicting a "hazard score". Re-running its preprocessing line by line on the same file shows where that number came from.

Check on the original notebook's pipelineResult
R² of a plain linear regression on the original target and features1.000
R² using only the three columns the target was built from1.000
R² once those columns are removed (sensors and weather only)0.721
Real hours deleted by the IQR filter29%
Hours above the NO2 limit deleted by the filter282 of 386 (73%)
Top 5% of CO hours deleted by the filter92%
Highest NO2 value left in the data223 µg/m³
Missing markers (-200) that stayed in CO as real values1,683
Missing NO2 readings replaced by the previous value1,642
NMHC column missing before it was forward-filled90%
Empty rows at the end of the file filled as copies of the last hour114

The hazard score was defined as a weighted sum of CO, NO2 and benzene, and those three columns were left in the feature matrix. Any model can recover a sum of its own inputs, so the score says nothing about predictive skill. With those columns removed, the same regression explains 72% of the variance, and that is still a same-hour estimate, not a forecast.

The outlier filter did the most damage to the goal of the project. It capped NO2 at 223.5 µg/m³ and CO at 5.6 mg/m³, which removed 29% of all hours and most of the pollution episodes. Most of the 1,898 "CO outliers" were not outliers at all: 1,683 of them were the file's missing-value marker, which had survived because that column was still text when -200 was replaced.

Everything below is rebuilt to avoid these problems: missing readings stay missing, no row is deleted for being high, every model is scored on months it has never seen, and naive baselines are scored on the same hours.

3. Understanding the data

Missing readings are not random

The NO2 analyser is missing 93% of the time at 03:00 and about 13% at its best hour (chi-square test of missingness against hour of day: p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.42). That is the signature of a nightly self-calibration cycle, so the gaps are scheduled, not random. Forward-filling would invent 1,642 NO2 values. This project never fills the target: hours without a reference reading are simply not scored.

Traffic drives a strong daily and weekly rhythm

Weekdays are more polluted than weekends for every pollutant tested. The comparison uses daily means, because consecutive hours are too correlated to count as independent observations.

PollutantWeekday meanWeekend meanDifference95% CICohen's dp (Holm)
NO2 (µg/m³)119.2100.019.2611.32 to 26.990.61< 0.001
CO (mg/m³)2.41.70.700.54 to 0.860.97< 0.001
NOx (ppb)270.4194.975.5342.30 to 108.330.50< 0.001

The sensors overlap heavily, and one of them is mislabelled

The first principal component of the five sensor channels carries 81% of their variance: they mostly measure one shared "traffic" signal. The channel sold as an NO2 sensor has a rank correlation of only 0.15 with reference NO2, and tracks temperature and humidity more closely than the gas. Useful calibration therefore has to combine channels. One more caution: reference benzene and sensor 2 have a rank correlation of 1.00, an exact one-to-one relationship, so benzene is left out of the calibration study because "predicting" it would prove nothing.

4. Calibrating the sensors, and keeping them calibrated

The scenario copies real deployments. The box is co-located with the reference station for the first 8 weeks, a calibration model is fitted, and the box is then scored on the remaining 6,337 hours.

For NO2, the nominal sensor alone is worse than predicting the average (R² -0.66). Combining all channels with temperature and humidity brings the error to 20.7 µg/m³ (18% of the mean). NOx is the opposite story: every model fitted in spring under-reads afterwards (overall bias of -159 ppb for ridge), because autumn and winter NOx levels are far above anything seen during co-location.

PollutantStatic | ridgeRolling | ridgeExpanding | ridgeStatic | treesRolling | treesExpanding | trees
CO (mg/m³)0.500.410.380.330.390.36
NO2 (µg/m³)20.6819.9519.7433.2820.0019.19
NOx (ppb)160.4055.4360.07140.9150.9352.98

Periodic recalibration cuts NOx error by 65% and helps CO with the linear model. It does little for NO2 (20.7 to 19.9 µg/m³ with ridge), and for CO a tree model fitted once was already as good as the refitted ones. Recalibration is not free in practice, since it needs fresh reference data, so the result argues for spending it where it pays: on NOx.

How long the co-location lasts matters less than what it covers. For CO with boosted trees, error on a fixed later window was 0.21 after 8 weeks, 0.40 after 12 and 0.20 after 16 mg/m³: more weeks did not reliably mean a better model.

Can drift be detected without reference data?

Three label-free monitors were tried: PSI, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and a domain classifier. They all fire almost immediately. Mean PSI is above the usual 0.25 alarm level in 11 of 12 blocks, and a classifier can tell every later block from the co-location period (AUC of at least 0.93). But neither signal ranks the blocks by how wrong the calibration actually was: rank correlations with the stale model's error range from -0.22 to 0.52, and none is significant with 12 blocks.

Input drift is not the same as performance drift. Seasons change temperature and humidity so much that the inputs always look different, whether or not the calibration still works. A drift alarm on inputs alone would have been permanently on. Knowing when to recalibrate needs at least occasional reference measurements.

5. Forecasting NO2 hours ahead

Models predict reference NO2 at 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 hours ahead from what is known at the time of the forecast: recent NO2, the value at the target's clock hour yesterday and last week, the sensor channels, weather, and the hour and day type being forecast. Evaluation is walk-forward over seven test months (September 2004 to March 2005): each month is predicted by models fitted only on earlier data. Tree hyperparameters were tuned once, inside the first training window.

HorizonBest modelBest naive baselineMAE improvement, µg/m³ (95% CI)

The learned models beat the best naive rule at every horizon, and the day-block bootstrap intervals exclude zero. The gain is largest at 3 hours and modest at 1 hour, where the last reading is already a strong forecast. A regularised linear model matches or beats gradient-boosted trees at every horizon beyond one hour. Trees cannot predict values above those they were trained on, and the test months are much more polluted than the training months, so the simpler model is the better choice here.

Errors are not spread evenly. On the hours that matter most, those above the 200 µg/m³ limit, the 6-hour ridge forecast is too low by 47 µg/m³ on average, and it is too high on clean hours. This pull towards the middle is what a model trained to minimise average error does, and it is the reason the alert system below is built on probabilities and not on the point forecast. By month, the worst is 2005-02 (ridge MAE 32.3), the most polluted month of the year.

Shuffling one input at a time on the final test month shows what the ridge model relies on: the value at the same clock hour yesterday, the time of day, and the value a week ago.

6. Prediction intervals that mean what they say

A forecast of 150 µg/m³ is far more useful with a range that can be trusted. Three ways of producing a 90% interval are compared on how often the truth actually falls inside.

HorizonInterval methodCoverage (target 90%)Mean width, µg/m³Worst month
1 hQuantile trees, raw79.8%5771% (2004-11)
1 hConformalized (static)86.2%7166% (2004-11)
1 hAdaptive conformal90.0%7789% (2004-12)
6 hQuantile trees, raw78.4%8266% (2004-11)
6 hConformalized (static)85.5%10862% (2004-11)
6 hAdaptive conformal89.8%11888% (2005-01)
24 hQuantile trees, raw71.3%7459% (2004-11)
24 hConformalized (static)86.0%11660% (2004-11)
24 hAdaptive conformal89.8%13489% (2004-12)
  • Quantile regression alone is overconfident. Its "90%" intervals contain the truth 78% of the time at 6 hours.
  • Standard conformal calibration fixes the average but not the bad months. Widening the intervals using the four weeks before each test month lifts coverage to 86%, yet it falls to 62% in 2004-11, when pollution rises faster than the calibration window can reflect.
  • Adaptive conformal prediction holds its promise every month. It widens after each miss and narrows after each hit, using only outcomes that would already be known. Coverage is 89.8% overall and never below 88% in any month. The price is honesty about the width: about 118 µg/m³ on average.

7. Warning before the limit is exceeded

The event is an hour with NO2 above 200 µg/m³, the EU hourly limit value. It is rare (374 of 4,283 test hours, 9%) and strongly seasonal: the first training window contained only 12 such hours. Two ways of estimating its probability are compared with two naive rules. Alerts are raised when the probability passes 0.17, the threshold implied by treating a missed exceedance as 5 times worse than a false alarm.

Alert methodBrier skillPR-AUCAlerts raisedPrecision %Recall %
Base rate (climatology)+0.000.120n/a0
Persistence (alert if over the limit now)-0.570.123502322
Classifier (boosted trees + Platt)+0.190.345703554
Forecast + residual distribution (ridge)+0.290.467113770

6 hours ahead, turning the regression forecast into a probability (by adding its recent errors to the forecast and counting how often the sum passes the limit) catches 70% of exceedances at 37% precision. A classifier trained directly on the rare event does worse (PR-AUC 0.34 against 0.46), most likely because it had almost no positive examples to learn from in the early months. Simply alerting when the current reading is over the limit catches 22%.

8. Unusual hours and typical days

Anomalies depend on context

The original project called any value outside a fixed range an outlier. Here an hour is flagged when it is far from what is typical for that clock hour and day type over the previous four weeks, measured with a robust z-score. Of 6,851 hours scored, 58 are flagged (49 high, 9 low). 62% of them sit inside the fixed IQR range and would have been missed, while 79% of the IQR "outliers" are ordinary for their hour and season.

Two kinds of day

Without being told the day of the week, clustering separates a commuter pattern with two rush-hour peaks from a late-evening pattern. The first is 95% weekdays, the second is 67% weekend days (chi-square p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.66). The weekdays that fall in the second cluster are candidates for holidays.

9. Limits and next steps

  • One station, one year, 2004 to 2005. Results describe this site. There is one winter, so seasonal conclusions rest on a single cycle.
  • No wind or rain. The weather channels are temperature and humidity only. Wind speed and mixing height are the main drivers of dispersion and would likely improve the 12 and 24-hour forecasts most.
  • The forecast uses reference NO2 as an input. That suits a station with an analyser. A sensor-only deployment would feed in calibrated sensor values, with the larger errors from section 4.
  • Intervals are wide. They are honest, but about 118 µg/m³ wide at 6 hours. Narrowing them needs better inputs, not a different interval method.
  • Next: repeat the study on a current low-cost network with public reference data, add weather forecasts as inputs, and test whether a small number of reference days per month is enough for recalibration.

10. Concept map

Data science conceptWhere it is demonstrated
Data quality and missing-data mechanismsSection 2 and 3: sentinel values, chi-square test of missingness by hour, no imputation of the target
Exploratory analysis and visualisationSection 3: seasonal profiles, autocorrelation, rank correlation
Statistical inferenceSection 3 and 5: Mann-Whitney tests with Holm correction, bootstrap and day-block bootstrap intervals, effect sizes
Dimensionality reductionSection 3: PCA of the sensor array
Regression and regularisationSection 4 and 5: linear, ridge with cross-validated penalty, gradient-boosted trees
Model selection and validationSection 5: walk-forward evaluation, gap-aware time-series cross-validation, naive baselines, leakage tests
Classification with rare eventsSection 7: precision, recall, PR-AUC, Brier score, probability calibration, cost-based threshold
ClusteringSection 8: k-means on daily profiles, silhouette selection, chi-square against day type
Anomaly detectionSection 8: robust z-scores against a seasonal expectation
Monitoring models after deploymentSection 4 and 6: drift metrics (PSI, KS, domain classifier), recalibration schedules, adaptive conformal prediction
ReproducibilityOne command reruns everything; fixed seeds; tests that fail if a feature can see the future
